clue.text: The anti-Protectionist stable?

definitions.meaning: Richard ..., the Victorian free-trade campaigner who fought the protectionist Corn Laws
read as ..., a lair for a cob, a stocky horse

explanation.surface: A question about where a free-trader keeps his horses.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Cobden led the Anti-Corn Law League against protection; split the surname as COB (a sturdy horse) plus DEN (its lodging) and it becomes a stable.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobden was the leading Victorian opponent of tariffs, and a den for a horse is a playful kind of stall.

clue.text: Scorn makes Constance notwithstanding play the deuce

indicators.note: read as 'not with standing': the name loses its stance, the word for a way of standing

parts.note: the deuce is the devil, whose part is to tempt

explanation.surface: Disdain drives a woman named Constance to cause mischief despite everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'notwithstanding' reads as 'not with standing', so CONSTANCE drops STANCE (a way of standing) to leave CON.
explanation.definitionFit: Disdain or derision for someone thought worthless.

clue.text: Hats for delivery men

definitions.meaning: hard round felt hats, also called derbies
in cricket the men who deliver the ball

explanation.surface: Headgear for men who deliver parcels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'delivery men' suggests couriers; in cricket the players who deliver the ball are the bowlers.
explanation.definitionFit: Round felt hats bear the name, and cricketers who deliver the ball do too.

clue.text: They explain symbols of power

definitions.meaning: people who expound or interpret ideas
in mathematics the small raised figures showing to what power a number is raised

explanation.surface: People who interpret the emblems of authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'power' sounds political; in mathematics it is the index written as a small raised number.
explanation.definitionFit: Interpreters of a doctrine are its expounders, and raised index numbers in algebra share the name.

clue.text: Mrs Loude arranged to do charring

indicators.note: arranged tells us the letters of the lady's name are to be set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A Mrs Loude is booked to come in and do the cleaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charring' looks like a charwoman's cleaning job, the part Mrs Loude seems hired for, but here it means scorching.
explanation.definitionFit: To smoulder is to burn slowly without flame, blackening and scorching whatever is alight.

clue.text: One who digs EEC affairs ?

parts.note: the EEC was the Common Market, and 'digs' means both likes and works the soil

explanation.surface: A fan of European Economic Community politics.
explanation.walkthrough: The EEC was called the Common Market, so a person who digs (tills) market plots is a grower of produce for sale.
explanation.definitionFit: A grower who cultivates vegetables and fruit for sale tills a plot devoted to the market.

clue.text: Your: one curl is curly, Wernerson

indicators.note: is curly says the letters of the following pieces twist into a new order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone admires a single curl on a man called Wernerson.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulric is the son of Werner in Byron's verse drama Werner; 'Wernerson' reads as a surname but means Werner's son.
explanation.definitionFit: In Byron's tragedy Werner, the title character's son bears this name.

clue.text: Books that best suit' bookworms ?

parts.note: condensed books, and also what a bookworm does when it eats books

explanation.surface: A question about which books avid readers like best.
explanation.walkthrough: Abridged volumes are called this, and a bookworm, as an insect, eats through and absorbs books.
explanation.definitionFit: Condensed books are this, and the verb describes a creature taking food in.

clue.text: One tress is awkward, not to lie down

indicators.note: is awkward tells us the letters before it are put in a clumsy new order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A single lock of hair that will not lie flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not to lie down' suggests unruly hair, but it means to refuse to submit.
explanation.definitionFit: To refuse to lie down, as in 'take it lying down', is to oppose or fight back.

clue.text: Mythical' antithesis' of an old tomato

definitions.text: Mythical' antithesis' of an old tomato

parts.words: Mythical' antithesis' of an old tomato
parts.note: an old name for the tomato was the love apple, and the golden apple of Greek myth caused strife

explanation.surface: A myth in which something is the very opposite of an ageing tomato.
explanation.walkthrough: The tomato was once called the 'love apple'; its opposite in myth is the golden apple that Eris threw, which led to the Trojan War.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden fruit thrown by Eris set the goddesses quarrelling, the reverse of an apple of love.

clue.text: The spread of intelligence

parts.note: intelligence is news, and a broadsheet is a large sheet spread open to read it

explanation.surface: A remark on how knowledge or cleverness spreads through society.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily paper is a printed sheet spread open and full of news, which is the old sense of intelligence.

clue.text: " Fear no more … the furious winter's —— " (Cymbeline)

parts.note: the missing word completes the dirge in Shakespeare's Cymbeline: 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun, Nor the furious winter's ...'

explanation.surface: A gap in a famous Shakespeare song for the solver to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The song is 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun' from Cymbeline; its second line ends 'Nor the furious winter's rages'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fury and storms are what a furious winter unleashes, so the plural noun completes the quotation.

clue.text: For always after a French season the Navy gets back there in France

parts.note: ete is French for summer
RN is the Royal Navy

indicators.note: gets back means the French word for there is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: la is French for there

explanation.surface: A navy returns to France after spending the summer there, for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets back' turns LA, the French for 'there', into AL to finish the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that lasts for always is everlasting, without end.

clue.text: Cuts taxes ?

definitions.meaning: to cut out surgically or remove a passage
duties levied on goods made at home

explanation.surface: A question whether spending cuts are really taxes in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: To remove by cutting is one sense, and duties charged on home-produced goods such as alcohol are the other.

clue.text: Having a leaning for some of Ezra's cantos

definitions.meaning: like the Leaning Tower in the Italian city of Pisa
Ezra Pound wrote a sequence called The ... Cantos

explanation.surface: A poet with a bias for some of Ezra Pound's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaning' suggests a preference, but it is the Leaning Tower; Pound wrote The Pisan Cantos while held near Pisa in 1945.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things from Pisa, home of the leaning tower, and names Pound's Pisan Cantos.

clue.text: Manual worker in harmonious conditions

parts.note: a keyboard on an organ is called a manual, and this worker labours among harmonies

explanation.surface: A labourer who enjoys a peaceful workplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manual worker' suggests a labourer, but the manuals are an organ's keyboards.
explanation.definitionFit: A church musician plays the keyboards called manuals, producing harmony as the job.

clue.text: Ena's troubled, taking fruit of the sapodilla

indicators.note: troubled tells us the letters of Ena's are stirred into a new order

parts.note: a berry is a small fruit, which the name takes on

explanation.surface: A woman named Ena is upset after picking the fruit of a tropical tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled' rearranges ENAS to NASE.
explanation.definitionFit: It is another name for the sapodilla, a tropical American tree and its sweet brown fruit.

clue.text: Each red's cunningly checked for hidden objects

indicators.note: cunningly suggests the letters of each and red's are craftily reordered

explanation.surface: Every communist is craftily frisked for concealed items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Each red's' looks like spies being frisked, but its letters rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To look thoroughly for concealed items, as police do when they frisk or comb a house.

clue.text: Dark horse lacking a stable?

definitions.meaning: a contender few expect to win
a horse without a stable would be left out in the open

explanation.surface: A question about an unfancied horse with no home stable.
explanation.definitionFit: A rank long shot in a race is called this, and a horse without shelter is literally out of doors.

clue.text: Tear off strip to do hair so it won't hang down

definitions.meaning: to scold, as in 'tear a strip off'

definitions.text: to do hair so it won't hang down
definitions.meaning: read as ..., plaiting the hair up

explanation.surface: Advice to tie hair up so it does not hang loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear off strip' is British slang for a scolding ('tear a strip off someone').
explanation.definitionFit: To reprimand sharply, and, split in two, to plait hair up off the neck.

clue.text: One dolorous that is not Dolores

parts.note: dolorous means sorrowful or sad
ie is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A gloomy woman who, oddly, is not called Dolores.
explanation.walkthrough: Dolores means 'sorrows', so a sad girl ought to bear that name; this one is a girl with a different name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a girl's name, so any girl with it is not called Dolores.

clue.text: Said to a companion on hearing a thud in the dusk?

definitions.text: Said to a companion on hearing a thud in the dusk?

parts.words: Said to a companion on hearing a thud in the dusk?
parts.note: after a thud you might ask 'D'you fall?', and at dusk moisture settles on the grass

explanation.surface: Someone hears a bump in the twilight and calls to a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sounds like the question 'D'you fall?', and moisture settling on the ground at dusk is literally what the word means.
explanation.definitionFit: The settling of moisture in the evening, sounding like the question a friend asks after a bump.

clue.text: Old Master who fought for U.S.A. to get essential oil

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
otto, or attar, is an essential oil from rose petals

explanation.surface: A great painter served with the American army and sought perfume.
explanation.definitionFit: Giotto di Bondone was a Florentine painter of the early Renaissance, an Old Master.

clue.text: Chest protector in a semi-round of drinks

indicators.note: in means the protector piece sits inside the jumbled letters
round tells us the letters of semi are to be turned about into a new order

parts.note: a bib protects the chest from spills

explanation.surface: Someone protects their shirt front during half a round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' rearranges SEMI to IMES, and 'in' puts BIB inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbibe is to take liquor in, so the verb means to drink.

clue.text: Daisy meets a Miss Wilfer

parts.note: from the music-hall song 'Daisy Bell' ('Daisy, Daisy, give me your answer, do')

explanation.surface: A girl named Daisy is introduced to a young woman called Wilfer.
explanation.walkthrough: Bella Wilfer is the heroine of Dickens's Our Mutual Friend; 'Daisy' gives BELL through the song 'Daisy Bell'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dickens's Our Mutual Friend, the heroine's first name is this; her surname is Wilfer.

clue.text: Put Rosamond in her place

parts.note: Fair Rosamond, mistress of Henry II, was said to be kept in a secret bower at Woodstock

explanation.surface: Someone tells a woman named Rosamond where she belongs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in her place' sounds like a rebuke, but Fair Rosamond's legendary place was a hidden bower, so to put her there is to enclose her in one.
explanation.definitionFit: To shelter someone in a leafy arbour or retreat, as legend says Henry II did with Rosamond.

clue.text: It was: a tortuous way to dreamland

definitions.text: It was: a tortuous way to dreamland

parts.words: It was: a tortuous way to dreamland
parts.note: recalls the First World War song 'There's a long, long ... a-winding into the land of my dreams'

explanation.surface: A remark that getting to sleep was a struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreamland' suggests falling asleep; the song 'There's a Long, Long Trail' has a winding path into the land of dreams.
explanation.definitionFit: A path is a way, and in the popular wartime song this winding one led to the land of dreams.

clue.text: Go beyond : one's' capacity, having finished a stretch of river

parts.note: something finished is over
a reach is a straight stretch of river

explanation.surface: Someone tries too hard after completing a length of a river.
explanation.definitionFit: To overreach is to attempt more than you can manage and fail.

clue.text: Spinsters enjoying domestic pensions ?

definitions.meaning: unmarried women past the usual age
former housemaids now living on a pension

explanation.surface: Unmarried women living off pensions from service.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderly unmarried women are called this, and retired servants who drew pensions would be aged housemaids.

clue.text: It is raised up for anyone to see"

definitions.text: It is raised up for anyone to see

parts.words: It is raised up for anyone to see
parts.note: a flap of skin that is lifted so that a person can see

explanation.surface: Something is held up high so everyone can see it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for anyone to see' suggests public display, but the thing must be raised so that its owner can see.
explanation.definitionFit: The fold of skin over the eye must be lifted before one can look out.
